chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
title: Never hearing the band: playing as one
summary: Jones says the section played with itself, gave each note its value and succeeded because of the lives they had lived together.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You've always told me about Walter Page. You know I knew him very well and he was like my master and I worshiped him. I know how you felt about him, but tell me a little more about him. I just want to hear from you because I could never get enough of listening to what you have to say about Walter Page and working with Bill Basie and Freddie Green in that tremendous rhythm section.

You see, Milt, when we went to work nobody spoke to us. We never played with the band; we played with ourselves. I don't care, with the four of us, if three people were down, one person was up. If two people, if three people, but one person on four cylinders, one person was up - we never heard the band. We concentrated on ourselves and you know what that concentration was - living with peoples that we had to satisfy. We were the frosting, fix not on the cake - we were the sugar. You taste a cake and you ain't got no sugar, the cake is not sweet. We had this thing but each one of us had had a personal life and we
incorporated that and we stayed that way.

You say you never heard the band and in the modern day of listening and playing the saying is that if you can't hear the band you're playing too loud. I can understand if you say that a band must play with the rhythm section, not the rhythm section play with the band, because the band is the timekeeper of the band.

That's right. A whole note gets four beats, a half note gets two, a quarter note gets one. There are four beats in the measure. We don't go with the joggin', time or money. Give each note its value, Little Bo-Peep,,the sheep it will follow. Just give a note its value, but we sit and we didn't go north, south, east, and west. We played as one. But what made us play as one, the kind of lives that we had lived as human beings, the elbows that we had touched out and reached. We brought that on the bandstand and we were strong enough to go through these things. There is a thing that even Mr. Bennie Moten had that I used to remember. They had Bus Moten, they had Basie jumping up and down -
